title: A Good Kind of Disruption
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart asks how school leaders get better, arguing that knowledge and relationships alone are insufficient because schools are complex systems whose problems are wicked, with no clear right answers and perennial uncertainty. Drawing on adult ego development theory, he contrasts earlier stages, which impose linearity and familiar rules (caricatured as the parachuted-in 'super head'), with later stages that tolerate ambiguity, see interconnectedness and co-construct meaning. His move is to identify disruptive experiences as a route to that development: encounters that push a leader to see a situation as someone at a later stage would. Talking with other leaders about shared problems is one rich source, though he notes such experiences seem to require personal salience to work. For leaders lacking those opportunities, he proposes a scaffold of self-prompts to use in the many daily decisions school leadership involves, such as zooming out, slowing down, weighing effects on others and seeking dissenting views.
points: Hart frames school leadership problems as wicked problems in complex systems, where small actions have large, unpredictable effects and it is hard even to tell when a problem is solved.
Adult ego development is offered as the lens: earlier stages seek linear fixes and familiar formulas, while later stages hold ambiguity and build understanding with others.
Disruptive experiences, deliberately sought rather than awaited, are proposed alongside knowledge-building and trust as a third route to leadership growth.
Peer conversation across schools can provide the necessary social condition for disruption, but only if leaders actually want the experience, which Hart calls personal salience.

He supplies concrete prompts for in-the-moment decisions, including slowing down, asking how an action affects staff, children, parents and trust, and checking understanding with someone likely to see it differently.
quotes: But of course, it is not as simple as that or any other suggestions that come to mind because schools are not simple, nor even complicated. They are complex, where small actions can have big consequences, where those consequences can be rather unpredictable, where the organisation may tend to organise itself and where its history influences its evolution.

In the lower stages of adult ego development, we’re concerned with the here and now, seeking to impose linearity or follow familiar rules, trying to make sense of a situation independently. One caricature of this is the hero headteacher, the super head, parachuted in to fix a school because they have formula that worked somewhere else. In the later stages of adult ego development, we seek understanding beyond the trigger incident, appreciating interconnectedness, we’re comfortable with ambiguity and letting our understanding gradually emerge, and we’re co-constructing meaning with others.

Simply talking with other leaders about common problems, whether those leaders are our colleagues and we’re talking about the same problem, or whether they are from different schools and talking about familiar problems that have manifested differently, is a rich opportunity. For those in school groups, this seems to be a great use of time for leaders to engage in knowledge animation and to expose different ways of thinking to provide a useful disruptive experience.

These researchers argue that such an experience needs to push us towards seeing a situation in a way that is aligned to how one with a higher stage of ego development would see it. The first step, I would argue, is to get to know how those people think!

Working with others creates what some would argue is a necessary condition for a disruptive experience. The tricky bit is that sometimes initiatives like this can work against another arguably necessary condition – personal salience. It appears that we have to want to have a disruptive experience for it to be disruptive!

So, if we do not have the connections to engage in such interaction, or we do not believe in the opportunities for development afforded to us, it makes sense to give ourselves a scaffold to nudge us in the right direction when the opportunity for a disruptive experience arises. And given the amount of problems that school leaders face hour by hour and the amount of decisions that are taken minute by minute, we’re not short of such opportunities.
